analysis.one_liner: Nullifies the FCC's net neutrality rules and bars the agency from reviving them without a new law.
analysis.headline: The bill to erase the FCC's 2015 net neutrality rules drew 54 Republican cosponsors and no Democrats, and died in the House Energy and Commerce Committee without ever getting a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have wiped out the FCC's February 26, 2015 order that reclassified broadband internet as a regulated telecommunications service — the legal basis for the net neutrality rules barring internet providers from blocking, slowing, or selling faster delivery to websites. It also would have barred the FCC from reissuing the rule, or anything substantially like it, unless Congress passed a new law specifically authorizing it, with a narrow exception for national security, public safety, and law enforcement rules. In practice, it was a repeal of the open internet rules at the request of the broadband industry.
analysis.who_benefits: Cable and telephone broadband providers gain the most: they would shed common-carrier obligations under Title II of the Communications Act, regaining freedom to manage traffic, offer paid fast lanes, and strike carriage deals with web companies without FCC review. Their gains are concentrated among a few dozen large carriers; big web platforms would keep enough bargaining power to protect themselves, while smaller sites would not.

how_it_helps.text: Voids the FCC's February 26, 2015 order reclassifying broadband internet access as a telecommunications service, lifting the Title II common-carrier obligations that underpinned the no-blocking, no-throttling, and no-paid-fast-lane rules.

Bars the FCC from reissuing the same rule, or one substantially similar, unless Congress enacts a law specifically authorizing it — locking in the lighter-touch regulatory regime rather than leaving the choice to the agency.

Leaves a narrow carve-out allowing FCC rules the agency deems necessary for national security, public safety, or law enforcement assistance, giving providers and security agencies a small preserved lane.

analysis.who_pays: Internet users and small online businesses would bear the cost. They would lose enforceable protections against their provider blocking or slowing sites, and websites that refused to pay for priority delivery could load more slowly — a price large platforms could absorb but startups, local news sites, and small merchants could not.

drawbacks.text: It would have wiped out the FCC's just-adopted open internet rules, leaving no enforceable ban on providers blocking, throttling, or charging websites for priority delivery — a fee structure large platforms could absorb but small sites and startups could not.

Supporters argued the 2015 order treated broadband like a Depression-era telephone utility, discouraged network investment, and let an unelected agency set national internet policy; the bill's answer was to nullify the rule and require a new act of Congress before the FCC could act again.

The bill was written as a total nullification rather than a replacement: it offered no alternative open-internet protections, so if the lighter-touch regime failed consumers, the only remedy would be new legislation clearing both chambers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits would have accrued to a concentrated set of large broadband carriers — lower regulatory risk and new freedom to monetize network position — while the costs would have been spread thin across every internet user and online business in the form of weaker enforceable protections and potential paid-prioritization fees. Weighed honestly, the bill traded a broad, diffuse consumer benefit for a concentrated industry gain, which is why it drew a purely Republican cosponsor list and strong opposition from internet companies and public interest groups.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its communications subcommittee in its first week, and no one ever scheduled it for a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Marsha Blackburn introduced the bill on March 3, 2015, three days after the Republican-sponsored attempt to overturn the FCC's open internet order failed in the Senate, and 54 House Republicans cosponsored it.
It was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee on March 3 and to the Subcommittee on Communications and Technology on March 6, 2015, and never advanced further.
The committee leadership never scheduled a markup or a floor vote, and the bill died there when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017, leaving the FCC's 2015 open internet rules in force.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Internet users, small websites, and online businesses are better off: the FCC's 2015 net neutrality rules remained in force because the repeal never advanced. Broadband providers, the intended beneficiaries, got nothing from this Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Internet users and small online businesses

for.name: Marsha Blackburn
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on March 3, 2015, days after the FCC's open internet order took effect, to void the reclassification of broadband and bar the FCC from restoring it.

for.name: 54 of 246 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; every cosponsor was a Republican and no Democrat signed on.

for.name: Broadband and cable industry
for.what_they_did: Fought the FCC's Title II reclassification and backed legislation to undo it, the goal this bill carried.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.role: Committee and Communications Subcommittee leadership (chair Fred Upton, R-MI)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing, markup, or floor vote; it sat in the communications subcommittee for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: President Barack Obama
against.what_they_did: Publicly pressed the FCC to adopt the Title II reclassification that this bill would nullify, and his administration backed the open internet rules.

against.name: Public interest groups and internet companies
against.role: Open internet advocates and web platforms
against.what_they_did: Campaigned for the FCC's open internet rules and against Title II repeal legislation like this bill.

sides.party_line_note: All 54 cosponsors were House Republicans and no Democrat sponsored the bill, while the Obama administration and Democratic-aligned advocacy groups defended the FCC rules the bill would repeal.

industries.note: The bill would have removed Title II common-carrier obligations — no blocking, no throttling, no paid fast lanes — freeing carriers to charge web services for priority delivery and manage traffic without FCC oversight. Their gain came directly at the cost of enforceable open-internet protections for their own customers.

industries.industry: Internet companies and web startups (edge providers)
industries.note: Websites and streaming services would have lost an enforceable right to reach users without discrimination and faced the risk of paying broadband providers for speed and access. Small sites and startups had the least leverage in that bargaining.
The bill strips the agency of its authority over broadband reclassification and locks that loss in by barring the FCC from reissuing the rule without a new act of Congress.
